      bypass (rs1_1_s1) -> 32-cell carry-chain branch comparator ->
      branch cond / misalign -> redirect -> u_if out.valid -> u_id
      flush -> sync RESET of ID/EX ctrl/rd/valid flops. Redirect is
      still in the ID/EX clear cone through if_stage.out.valid and
      hazard flush_id.
  (B) path 3 (8 cells): ID/EX.op_b_hit -> alu_b bypass -> adder SUM
      (u_alu n90_s2) -> FIVE LUT levels (n705_s18/s10/s4/s1/s0) ->
      EX/MEM.alu_result. That is the 11-way alu_op case mux, then the
      div_done mux, then the mul_sel mux.
  (C) paths 4, 6-8, 11-15 (5 cells): EX/MEM.reg_write (fanout 133) ->
      alu_a bypass -> DSP (3.76 ns) -> 2 LUTs -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
LESSONS r2s0 says to trim every tied path in one iteration: cutting
only one of A/B/C leaves Fmax flat. Every family ends at an EX-owned
result. Rather than tweak each LUT, this change moves work across
pipeline boundaries: the squash of the wrong-path instruction moves one
stage later, and MUL/DIV write their result one stage later.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three structural moves in one diff. The target cycle cost is under +1%,
and every EX endpoint should have at most 2 LUT levels after its carry
chain or DSP.

1. Registered wrong-path squash (cuts A). The redirect no longer kills
   the IF word or clears ID/EX. if_stage.out.valid depends only on the
   imem stall. hazard flush_if = imem_stall, and
   flush_id = load_use && !dmem_stall. On a redirect, ID/EX captures the
   wrong-path word normally, and a new 1-bit flop records the kill:
   `squash_q <= redirect` when ID/EX captures (!stall_id), and it holds
   otherwise. It is logically part of ID/EX. In EX, squash_q gates the
   redirect (redirect &= !squash_q), clears EX/MEM valid,
   ctrl.reg_write, mem_read and mem_write (a flop -> sync-clear path,
   not on the compare cone), and gates is_div (a wrong-path DIV must
   neither start the divider nor raise div_busy). The penalty is still
   exactly 1 bubble per taken branch or jump, so cycles do not change.
   The redirect then fans out only to the PC mux (33 loads) plus
   squash_q.
   Also shorten the redirect cone itself (lessons r4s2):
     - ID computes pc + imm (pc is a flop, imm comes from the LFSR/imem
       flop) into a new ID/EX.pc_imm. The branch and JAL target is that
       flop. Only JALR keeps the EX rs1 + imm adder.
       redirect_target = is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],0} : pc_imm_q.
     - Register one-hot compare selects in ID (sel_eq, sel_lt, sel_ltu,
       cmp_inv), so cond = cmp_inv ^ (sel_eq&eq | sel_lt&lt |
       sel_ltu&ltu), which is 1-2 LUTs after the carry chains.
     - A branch/JAL target is misaligned iff imm[1] (pc is always
       4-aligned). Register br_ok = is_branch && !imm[1] and
       jal_ok = is_jump && !is_jalr && !imm[1]. Only the JALR check
       uses the low bits of the bypassed rs1. Only a misaligned jump
       clears reg_write, so the branch compare stays out of
       EX/MEM.reg_write (a branch never writes rd).
       EX/MEM.pc_next / is_illegal feed only RVFI and are pruned.
2. MUL/DIV results moved to a MEM late select (cuts C and part of B).
   EX/MEM gets a new xres field:
   `xres <= div_done ? div_result : mul_out` (DSP -> 1 LUT -> flop, or
   let Gowin absorb it into the DSP output register). ID/EX gets a
   registered `late` bit (decoded mem_read || MUL* || DIV*).
   The existing load-use compare in hazard_unit uses `id_ex.late`
   instead of `id_ex.ctrl.mem_read`: the same LUT count, and a
   consumer directly behind a MUL takes one bubble. Then MUL is in
   EX/MEM and ID's existing 2-ahead forward supplies it through
   mem_result. The mem_stage result becomes
   mem_result = mem_to_reg ? load_data : (res_late ? xres : alu_result),
   with the BSRAM load data selected last. res_late (MUL/DIV) is a
   registered bit. EX/MEM.alu_result no longer carries MUL/DIV, so the
   EX 1-ahead bypass never sees them; the interlock guarantees no
   consumer needs them 1-ahead. r3s1 measured this kind of MUL-use
   interlock at about +0.8% cycles (4.527M vs 4.492M). That is far
   cheaper than r1s1's 2-stall MUL unit, and MUL stays a 1-cycle
   issue.
3. One-hot AND-OR base ALU (cuts the rest of B). ID registers one-hot
   result selects instead of relying on the 5-bit alu_op case mux:
   sel_arith (ADD/SUB/LUI/AUIPC/JAL link; LUI becomes ADD with
   op_a pre-selected to 0 in ID), a 2-bit logic code (00 = off,
   AND/OR/XOR, folded into one LUT4 per bit), sel_shift (masked in the
   shifter's last level), sel_slt/sltu, and a registered `sub` bit
   (SUB/SLT/SLTU). SLT/SLTU come from the shared subtract carry chain
   (sign/overflow and carry-out), not from separate comparators.
   result[i] = (sel_arith & sum[i]) | logic_m[i] | shift_m[i] is one
   LUT4 after the adder SUM (bit 0 adds the slt bit). That is about
   5 -> 1-2 levels.
Expected Fmax: the new worst paths should be the EX 2:1 bypass ->
shifter or adder -> 1-2 LUTs, the bypass -> comparator -> redirect ->
PC mux, and ID-side paths (LFSR -> LUT-RAM read -> forward -> ID/EX,
and load-use -> stall CE). Each is about 1.5-2 ns shorter than
today's 10.7 ns, which gives about 105-112 MHz, against a cycle cost
of about +0.8%. Net +11-18%. Before handing off, run `make timing`
and fix any new tied family the same way.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r5s1 (improvement, +14.43%): The r3s1 restructure that lost at ~76 MHz won once it was rebased on r4s1, reaching ~108 MHz if cycles rose by r3s1's ~0.8%, which is inside its 105–112 MHz estimate and above the ~103 MHz of r5s0, which made the same one-hot ALU and squash cuts but kept the DSP in the EX result; the restructure moves the MUL/DIV result to a MEM late select behind a 1-cycle use interlock (the existing load-use compare keys on a registered `late` bit, so it costs no extra LUTs) and adds a squash_q flop that kills the wrong-path word in EX, so the redirect drives only the PC mux and one flop and a taken branch still costs 1 bubble; the lesson is that an idea which lost only because a sibling fixed a shared path head is not refuted, so re-run `make timing` on each new champion and re-queue the idea once its tails become the tied worst paths; squash_q must also gate EX/MEM valid, reg_write, mem_read and mem_write, and the divider start, or a wrong-path DIV raises div_busy.

title: Zero-bubble IF predictor (predecode + pc+imm + 64-entry BTFN-disagree BHT) stacked on r4s1, with redirect taken off the ID/EX clear via a squash_q flop
motivation:
The champion (r4s1, 94.2 MHz, 4,491,817 cycles, 209.72) still resolves
every control transfer in EX, so each taken branch, JAL and JALR costs one
bubble (~357k bubbles, ~8% of cycles). The predictor has been measured
three times: r1s2 and r4s2 both cut cycles to ~4.194M (-6.6%). It lost
each time only to a same-round timing sibling. LESSONS r4s2 says to stack
it on r4s1 now.
The champion's worst path is the redirect cone itself (16.04 ns, 37 cells):
EX/MEM.alu_result -> EX 2:1 bypass -> 32-bit compare -> redirect/out.valid
logic in u_if -> ID/EX ctrl sync-clear (u_id reg_q.ctrl.branch_op). So a
predictor that also shortens the redirect cone gains IPC and Fmax together.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Port the r4s2 predictor onto r4s1 and cut the redirect -> ID/EX clear.
1. IF: predecode io_imemData (JAL; BRANCH with funct3 not 2/3), select the
   J/B immediate on instr[3], one pc+imm adder, 64x2-bit BTFN-disagree BHT
   in flops indexed by pc[7:2] (reset 0), dir = instr[31] ^ ctr[1].
   pred_taken = !imm[1] && (is_jal || (is_br && dir)). PC next-state has
   redirect as the last select: redirect ? redirect_target :
   stall ? pc : pred_taken ? pred_tgt : pc+4. IF emits pred_taken and
   alt_pc (the not-predicted path).
2. ID: precompute br_inv = funct3[0] ^ pred_taken, br_redir = is_branch &&
   !imm[1], and a one-hot EQ/LT/LTU compare select. Capture alt_pc.
3. EX: redirect = !squash_q && in.valid && ((br_redir && (base_cmp ^ br_inv))
   || (is_jalr && !jalr_sum[1])). redirect_target = is_jalr ?
   {jalr_sum[31:1],0} : alt_pc. An aligned JAL never redirects.
   branch_taken, pc_next, the misalign traps and RVFI stay the same.
4. Squash flop, not a clear: squash_q <= stall_ex_mem ? squash_q :
   redirect. When squash_q is set, the wrong-path instruction in EX gets
   valid, reg_write, mem_read and mem_write cleared going into EX/MEM. It
   cannot redirect, start the divider, raise div_busy or update the BHT.
   IF out.valid and flush_id no longer depend on redirect, so the
   fanout-150+ ID/EX control clear leaves the redirect cone. Redirect now
   drives only the PC D-mux, squash_q and the registered BHT update.
   Mispredict penalty stays at 1 bubble.
Correctness notes: a squashed instruction's registered rs?_hit_ex is safe,
because EX/MEM.reg_write (cleared on squash) qualifies it. The ID 2-ahead
forward uses the same gated reg_write. A squashed LOAD in EX can raise a
false load-use stall, which costs one cycle and is rare. Gate
id_ex_mem_read with !squash_q only if it stays off the critical path. In
the timed harness io_imemData is an LFSR flop and imem_addr only feeds an
XOR, so the new IF path runs from a flop to the PC flop.
Expected: cycles ~4.19M (-6.6%). The redirect cone drops from ~5 LUTs plus
a fanout-157 route to about 2 LUTs into the PC mux, so Fmax should hold at
or above 94 MHz and fitness should rise ~7-10%. If make timing puts the IF
predecode -> pc+imm -> PC path near the top, use two parallel adders
(pc+immB and pc+immJ) and select after them.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r5s2 (regression, +4.99%): Stacking the zero-bubble IF predictor on r4s1, with a squash_q flop instead of the redirect -> ID/EX clear, netted +4.99% (220.18 vs 209.72), short of the expected +7–10%; if cycles fell to r1s2's ~4.19M, Fmax slipped from 94.2 to ~92.3 MHz instead of rising, most likely because the squash and branch-select cuts removed only the redirect tail and left the ALU-result and in-EX DSP tails that r5s0 found tied with it on r4s1 (cutting one of several tied paths buys nothing, as r2s0 found), while the IF predecode/pc+imm/BHT logic cost ~2%; this makes five predictor ports (r1s2, r2s2, r3s2, r4s2, r5s2) that each delivered roughly their ~6.6% cycle cut and then lost to a same-round timing sibling (here r5s1, +14.4%, which already has the same squash_q), so stop racing the predictor against timing work and apply only its IF predecode + BHT, the ID alt_pc/br_inv/one-hot compare precompute, and the mispredict-only redirect onto the r5s1 champion, expecting about +4–5%, then check `make timing` at ~108 MHz (9.3 ns) for the imem_data -> predecode -> pc+imm -> PC path and, if it is near the top, switch to the two-adder variant.

title: Cut all three tied 9.6 ns EX tails at zero cycle cost: CE-free PC (redirect is the last select), 2-LUT branch cond on one compare chain, 1-LUT DSP tail (DIV result read in MEM), pre-masked 3-level shifter
motivation:
I ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (r5s1, placement option
0 = 103.6 MHz, 4.53M cycles). The top 25 setup paths all fall within
0.04 ns of each other (9.58-9.62 ns data delay). They come from three
families, and per lesson r2s0 all three must be cut in one diff:
 (A) paths 1-13, 15-24, BRANCH -> PC (37 cells, 9.618 ns):
     EX/MEM.alu_result_1 -> 1.43 route -> rs1 bypass LUT -> 1.05 route ->
     32-cell compare carry chain (1.6 ns) -> 1.78 route -> THREE LUTs
     (u_if n69_s23/s12/s5 = cond select, br_ok&&cond, jal/jalr OR,
     squash) -> redirect (fanout 33) -> 0.68 route -> pc_30_s3, the
     PC clock-enable LUT (CE = redirect | !stall, fanout 30) -> 0.80
     route -> pc_*/CE. Path 4 goes through the D mux instead
     (9.608 ns). So after the chain there are 4 LUT levels and two
     ~0.7 ns high-fanout routes.
 (B) path 14, DSP (6 levels, 9.586 ns): alu_result_31 -> alu_a bypass
     LUT (fo 16) -> the sign-extension LUT n496 ({mul_sa & a[31]},
     fo 4 -> DSP A[33] fo 72) -> 1.09 route -> DSP 3.76 ns -> LUT
     (mul_hi ? hi : lo) -> 0.41 route -> LUT (div_done ? div_result :
     mul_out) -> EX/MEM.xres.
 (C) path 25, ALU shifter (9 levels, 9.581 ns): alu_result_16 ->
     alu_a bypass LUT (fo 7) -> 2.15 ns route -> SEVEN LUTs
     (u_alu n45_s3, n45_s1, alu_base_23_s5, alu_base_31_s6/s4/s1/s)
     -> EX/MEM.alu_result_31. That is the 5-stage binary barrel
     shifter, then the sel_sll/sel_sr masks and the 5-input AND-OR.
Every family has at least one LUT level plus about 0.7 ns of route that
exists only for how the logic is written, not for what it has to compute.
Cycles do not change, so each ns cut from the worst path adds about 10%
to fitness.

This change touches timing only. Forwarding, interlocks, the 1-bubble
taken-branch penalty, the MUL-use interlock and the divider FSM all stay
the same, and cycles stay at ~4.53M. The goal is to get every family
below ~8.9 ns (about 112 MHz, +7-9%).

A. Redirect -> PC (family A)
 A1. CE-free PC. In if_stage write
       pc_seq = pc + {29'b0, !stall, 2'b0};   // stall folded into the increment
       pc    <= reset ? RESET_PC : (redirect ? redirect_target : pc_seq);
     There is no `else if (!stall)` hold, so synthesis cannot pull out a
     clock-enable, and redirect becomes the last 2:1 select before each
     PC D pin (one LUT3/bit). This removes the CE LUT pc_30_s3 and its
     fanout-30 route, about 0.3 + 0.8 ns. The stall -> 30-bit carry
     chain is ~4.5 ns and far off the critical path. Redirect keeps
     priority over stall, as before. If Gowin still infers a CE, put
     (* syn_keep = 1 *) on pc_seq.
 A2. Two LUTs from the chain to redirect. In ID, register
     cmp_use_eq (BEQ/BNE), cmp_inv (funct3[0]) and cmp_signed
     (BLT/BGE). Also register precombined go bits: br_go = br_ok,
     jal_go = jal_ok. squash stays its own flop but ANDs in with the
     early terms. In EX:
       lt   = unsigned compare of {rs1[31]^cmp_signed, rs1[30:0]} vs
              {rs2[31]^cmp_signed, rs2[30:0]}, so one carry chain serves
              BLT/BGE/BLTU/BGEU. Bit 31 enters the chain last, so the
              XOR is off the path.
       eq   = rs1 == rs2 (parallel LUT tree or NE chain, whichever
              synthesis picks)
       cond = cmp_inv ^ (cmp_use_eq ? eq : lt);   // one LUT4, 2 late inputs
       redirect = (!squash & (jal_go | jalr_ok)) | (!squash & br_go & cond)
     The early OR terms are computed off flops, so redirect is
     LUT4(cond) plus one LUT (or MUX2_LUT5) after the chains, not three
     LUTs. This also removes one of the three 32-bit compare chains
     (lt and ltu are merged), which shortens the rs1/rs2 bypass fanout
     route that feeds the chains. Keep the misalign-trap semantics:
     misalign_branch uses the same cond, and a branch compare never
     reaches reg_write.
 A3. (optional) If A1+A2 leave family A still on top, give the compare
     its own copy of the rs1/rs2 bypass (syn_keep), so the chain input
     route is not shared with the AGU, JALR, divider and store-data
     loads.

B. DSP -> xres (family B)
 B1. Drop the div_done mux from the DSP tail. The divider's result_q
     flop does not change between FIX and the next division's FIX (at
     least 34 cycles later), so the DIV* in MEM can read it directly.
     Add an EX/MEM is_div bit, and in mem_stage use
       mem_result = mem_to_reg ? load_data
                  : res_late ? (is_div_q ? div_result : xres) : alu_result
     These selects are flops, and the load data still comes last. xres is
     then just mul_hi ? prod[63:32] : prod[31:0], one LUT3 after the
     DSP, which saves one LUT plus ~0.4 ns of route. The ALTOPS branch
     is unchanged: divider.sv still produces its stand-in in result_q.
     RVFI rs1/rs2_rdata for DIV* still come from div_a/div_b when
     div_done, as today.
 B2. Build the DSP sign-extension bits straight from flops, parallel to
     the bypass:
       a_sx = mul_sa & (fwd_a ? fwd_ex_mem[31] : op_a[31])
       b_sx = mul_sb & (fwd_b ? fwd_ex_mem[31] : op_b[31])
     Each is one LUT4 beside the alu_a/alu_b[31] bypass LUT, not a
     second LUT after it (n496). Use syn_keep if synthesis re-shares
     alu_a[31]. That saves ~0.45 ns + 0.66 ns route.

C. Shifter -> alu_result (family C)
 C1. Pre-mask and give the shifter its own bypass copy. In EX compute
       sll_in = {32{sel_sll}} & (fwd_a ? fwd_ex_mem : op_a)
       sr_in  = {32{sel_sr}}  & (fwd_a ? fwd_ex_mem : op_a)
     Each is one LUT4/bit off flops (fwd_a is one LUT off flops). The
     shifter outputs are then already zero when not selected, so the
     sel_sll/sel_sr output masks disappear. The shifter's input net is
     also no longer the fanout-7 alu_a net with its 2.15 ns route.
     SRA fill = sel_sra & sr_in[31] (sel_sra registered in ID).
 C2. Write both shifters as radix-4 stages: shamt[1:0] (4:1),
     shamt[3:2] (4:1), then shamt[4] (2:1). Code them as explicit
     2-bit case muxes so Gowin maps each 4:1 onto LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5.
     That gives 3 levels instead of 5.
 C3. base_out = sum_m | logic_m | sll_out | sr_out | slt_bit, where
     sum_m and logic_m are already masked by registered selects. This is
     a flat 4-5 input OR, which is two LUT levels at most, and
     SLT/SLTU only reach bit 0.
 Expected: bypass + 3 shifter levels + 2 OR levels, down from bypass +
 7, so family C loses about 1.2-1.5 ns.

Why this should win now: the three families are tied within 0.04 ns, so
the gain is capped by whichever family ends up slowest. I expect A to
lose ~1.0-1.4 ns (A1 + A2), B ~1.0 ns (B1 + B2) and C ~1.2 ns.
Whatever is next should then sit near 8.6-8.9 ns (AGU -> dmem BSRAM
address, ID's mem_result -> ID/EX forward), which gives Fmax
~112-116 MHz at unchanged cycles: fitness ~247-258, +3-8% by the
path math and +7% as the central estimate. Run `make timing
TARGET=bench` after the diff. If one family is still within 0.1 ns of
the old worst, apply its optional cut (A3), or duplicate the
EX/MEM.alu_result flops that feed the bypasses (syn_preserve), before
handing off.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r6s0 (regression, -3.35%): Cutting all three tied ~9.6 ns EX tail families on r5s1 in one zero-cycle diff (CE-free PC with redirect as the last select, one XOR-biased unsigned compare chain with the go bits precombined in ID, DIV result read from the divider flop in MEM so the DSP tail is one LUT3, flop-side sign-extension bits, pre-masked radix-4 shifters) lowered Fmax instead of raising it the estimated ~7%: at the unchanged ~4.53M cycles, 231.94 means ~105.0 MHz against the champion's 108.66; the likely reason is that the "tie" was measured on placement option 0 (103.6 MHz), while the scored champion Fmax is the best placement seed (logged Fmax has matched the top of each seed range since r2s0), so the ~5% spread between seeds was as large as the ~1 ns the LUT counts promised, and the extra logic (added operand copies, pre-masked shifter inputs and more loads on the bypass nets) cost routing that LUT counting does not see, while the next paths (AGU -> dmem BSRAM, ID mem_result -> ID/EX) were estimated at 8.6–8.9 ns but never measured; near 9 ns, check `make timing` on the actual diff across all scored seeds before handing off, and favor moves that take work out of the stage (as r5s1 did) over more LUT trimming.

title: Tail-side 1-ahead bypass: forward the EX ALU output straight into the ID/EX operand flops, delete the EX bypass muxes so every EX consumer starts at a flop
motivation:
I ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion r5s1 (placement option 0,
103.6 MHz; 9.6 ns data delay against 5 ns with 2.09+3.24 ns of clock
insertion). The worst 25 paths are three families tied within 0.07 ns, and
all three share the same head: EX/MEM.alu_result (Q) -> 1.4 ns route -> EX
1-ahead bypass LUT (rs1_1_s1 / alu_a_*), 0.37-0.55 ns, high fanout ->
1.0-2.1 ns route.
  (A) paths 1-13, 15-24 (9.618 ns, 37 cells): bypass -> 32-cell compare
      carry chain (1.6 ns) -> 1.78 ns route -> cond/redirect LUTs
      (u_if n69_s23/s12/s5, fanout 33) -> PC CE LUT (pc_30_s3, fanout 30)
      -> u_if/pc CE.
  (B) path 14 (9.586 ns): bypass alu_a_31 -> mul sign-extension LUT ->
      DSP (3.76 ns) -> 2 LUTs -> EX/MEM.xres.
  (C) path 25 (9.581 ns): bypass alu_a_16 (fanout 7, 2.15 ns route) ->
      three shifter LUT levels -> four result-OR LUTs (alu_base_31_s6/s4/s1/s)
      -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
LESSONS r2s0/r5s0 say that cutting only one of several tied paths leaves
Fmax flat. The only element all three families share is the EX-side
forwarding mux and the EX/MEM.alu_result -> bypass route, so a structural
change that removes that head is needed. Trimming each tail separately
would not do it.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move the last remaining EX-side bypass (1-ahead, EX/MEM.alu_result ->
rs1/rs2/alu_a/alu_b) from the head of EX to the tail of EX. ID/EX captures
the 1-ahead producer's result directly from the EX ALU output (alu_base,
combinational, the same value that EX/MEM.alu_result would latch). Then
ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val/op_a/op_b are fully resolved flops, and EX has no
forwarding muxes at all. This is register-read-stage bypassing (r4s1)
carried to its end point: bypass all four distances (1-, 2-, 3-ahead)
before the ID/EX register.

Mechanics (cycle count unchanged: ID/EX captures only when EX/MEM also
advances, so the producer in EX is always exactly the 1-ahead one):
  - ID keeps rs1_hit_ex / rs2_hit_ex (ID/EX.rd vs raw rs fields) and
    qualifies them with the live EX write enable, which is EX's
    ctrl_next.reg_write (already includes !squash, !misaligned-jump,
    !div_busy; the jalr_sum[1] term is a 2-bit carry, short). A late
    producer (LOAD/MUL/DIV) never hits: load-use bubbles the consumer and
    it picks the value up next cycle from the existing 2-ahead mem_result
    forward. Also mask the hit with !late so the select stays exact.
  - Capture priority: 1-ahead alu_base > 2-ahead mem_result > regfile
    (write-first 3-ahead) > constants. Put alu_base in the LAST 2:1 LUT in
    front of each ID/EX flop (it is the latest arrival), with the other
    inputs pre-muxed. op_a/op_b take alu_base only when the operand is a
    register (the existing !a_is_const / !b_is_const masks).
  - EX: delete the four bypass muxes and forward_unit.sv. The branch
    comparator, JALR adder, AGU, divider operands, store data, DSP inputs
    and ALU all read ID/EX flops. EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data <= the
    ID/EX values, and RVFI rdata is unchanged in meaning.
    Drop rs1_hit_ex/rs2_hit_ex/op_a_hit/op_b_hit from id_ex_t.
Effect per family:
  (A) loses the bypass LUT and ~2.4 ns of routing at its head. The compare
      chain now starts at ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val.
  (B) loses the bypass LUT and its route. Gowin can now absorb the MUL sign
      extension and the op_a/op_b flops into DSP input registers or place
      them next to the DSP.
  (C) becomes ID/EX.op_a -> ALU -> alu_base -> one 2:1 LUT -> ID/EX.op_a.
      The mux moves from head to tail, and the head no longer has the
      fanout-7 bypass LUT and 1.4 ns route. C then becomes the only
      remaining loop and has to be trimmed in the same diff (LESSONS
      r2s0), as follows.
Also trim the tails that stay in the same diff:
  - C: make the ALU result one LUT4 after the adder SUM and after the last
    shifter level. Mask each shifter (sel_sll / sel_sr) at its first level
    (ID can register a zeroed operand when the op is not a shift), fold
    slt/sltu into bit 0 only, and pre-OR logic_m with the arith term so
    bit i = OR4(arith|logic, sll_last, sr_last) (the shifter's
    4:1 levels can use MUX2_LUT5). Target: at most 5 LUT levels op_a ->
    alu_base, then 1 mux LUT.
  - A: make the PC flop always-enabled (D = redirect ? target :
    (stall ? pc : pc + 4), redirect as the last select). This deletes the
    CE LUT (pc_30_s3, fanout 30) and its 0.8 ns route from the redirect
    tail. Keep redirect overriding stall.
Expected: A and B fall to about 7-7.5 ns data delay. C falls to about
8-8.5 ns with the tail mux and the tree trim. The new limiter should be C
or the ID capture path (imem BSRAM -> rs compare -> select). That is about
115-122 MHz against 108.7 at the same 4.53M cycles, so +6-12%. Run
`make timing` before handing off. If an ID-side path (imem_data ->
rs-compare -> alu_base select) is now on top, register-precompute the
select, e.g. by splitting the hit into (rd match) and (reg_write), with
reg_write as the last LUT input.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r6s1 (regression, -6.98%): Moving the last EX bypass (1-ahead) from the head of EX to the ID/EX inputs, so that EX's combinational ALU output (alu_base) is the last 2:1 select in front of the rs1_val/rs2_val/op_a/op_b flops and EX has no forwarding muxes, fell to ~101 MHz at the unchanged ~4.53M cycles (223.23 against the champion's 108.66 MHz), and same-round sibling r6s0 made the overlapping tail trims (CE-free PC, pre-masked shifters) without the move and reached ~105 MHz, so the move itself most likely cost about another 4 MHz; the reason is that ALU -> bypass mux -> ALU is a one-cycle recurrence that retiming cannot shorten: moving the mux from head to tail keeps the ALU, the mux and a route inside the cycle, and it also puts up to 128 more ID-side mux loads on alu_base, placed near the imem BSRAM and LUT-RAM regfile, whose select arrives late (raw imem rs compare ANDed with EX's live reg_write, which carries squash, misaligned-jump and div_busy); to remove a bypass head that several tied paths share, take consumers out of the 1-ahead loop (for example, a 1-cycle use interlock for the branch-compare, DSP or AGU consumers, as r5s1 did for MUL) rather than relocating the mux.

title: PC-indexed 32-entry LUT-RAM BTB (zero-bubble taken branches/JAL, no imem_data predecode), verified in EX with replay
motivation:
Five zero-bubble predictor ports (r1s2..r5s2) each delivered the ISS-trace
cycle cut (~297k of ~4.49M cycles, -6.6%: every taken branch / JAL
currently costs one EX-redirect bubble) and then gave most of it back in
Fmax. All five used the same front end: predecode the fetch word
(io_imemData), compute pc+imm in IF and put it into the PC mux. That
hangs a decoder, a 32-bit adder and the direction logic on the
next-PC -> PC / io_imemAddr path. LESSONS says to apply that design
again on r5s1 and expect +4-5%, which is below the 4.6% acceptance bar.
The champion (r5s1, 108.66 MHz, 4.528M cycles) has its worst path at
EX/MEM.alu_result -> bypass -> branch compare / JALR adder -> redirect
-> u_if/pc (37 cells). A predictor that adds nothing to that path and
keeps its own next-PC logic short and off imem_data can get the whole
~6% IPC gain without losing Fmax. A branch target buffer indexed by the
registered PC does this. Its lookup starts at the PC flop, reads a small
LUT-RAM, and needs no adder and no instruction bits.

hypothesis.motivation:
Five zero-bubble predictor ports (r1s2..r5s2) each delivered the ISS-trace
cycle cut (~297k of ~4.49M cycles, -6.6%: every taken branch / JAL
currently costs one EX-redirect bubble) and then gave most of it back in
Fmax. All five used the same front end: predecode the fetch word
(io_imemData), compute pc+imm in IF and put it into the PC mux. That
hangs a decoder, a 32-bit adder and the direction logic on the
next-PC -> PC / io_imemAddr path. LESSONS says to apply that design
again on r5s1 and expect +4-5%, which is below the 4.6% acceptance bar.
The champion (r5s1, 108.66 MHz, 4.528M cycles) has its worst path at
EX/MEM.alu_result -> bypass -> branch compare / JALR adder -> redirect
-> u_if/pc (37 cells). A predictor that adds nothing to that path and
keeps its own next-PC logic short and off imem_data can get the whole
~6% IPC gain without losing Fmax. A branch target buffer indexed by the
registered PC does this. Its lookup starts at the PC flop, reads a small
LUT-RAM, and needs no adder and no instruction bits.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a direct-mapped 32-entry BTB, looked up by the registered PC in the
same cycle as the fetch. Verify its predictions one stage later, from
flops only, so the EX redirect cone gets no deeper.

IF (new rtl/btb.sv, instantiated in if_stage):
- Entry = {tag = pc[14:7] (8b), target[19:2] (18b), ctr (2b)} in a
  (* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *) array (RAM16SDP4: async read,
  1 sync write port, about 14 cells). Index = pc[6:2]. A separate
  32-bit valid vector in reset-cleared flops, so no RAM reset is needed.
  With this tag, lookups are exact for code below 32 KB. link.ld's FLASH
  region is 128K; if CoreMark's .text is larger than 32 KB, widen the
  tag to pc[16:7]. Aliasing is only a performance issue, because the EX
  check below catches it.
- hit = valid[idx] && tag == pc[14:7]; pt (predicted taken) = hit &&
  ctr[1]. next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target
                             : (pt ? {12'b0, tgt, 2'b00} : pc + 4).
  The redirect mux stays the LAST select in front of the PC flop, so the
  current worst path gains no level. The new PC -> LUT-RAM -> tag
  compare -> 2:1 -> 2:1 path is about 6 LUT levels, all from flops.
- if_id_t gets pt, hit, ctr[1:0], pred_tgt[19:2]. The PC advances on
  exactly the cycles when ID/EX captures a valid word (the stall_if and
  stall_id conditions already line up), so the captured prediction is
  always the one the PC followed.

ID (id_stage): register pt / hit / ctr / pred_tgt in ID/EX. pt joins the
control-only clear group (bubble, imem-stalled word, load-use slot).
This clear is required: a garbage word with pt=1 must not replay.
Fold the prediction into the registered selects, so EX sees the same
shape as today:
  cmp_inv <= funct3[0] ^ pt   (a predicted-taken branch redirects on !cond)
  jal_ok  <= JAL && !imm[1] && !pt   (a correctly predicted JAL never redirects)
Also register pc+4 (the incrementer is already in IF) so EX can use it
as the fall-through target.

EX (ex_stage), all new terms come from ID/EX flops:
- match = (pc_imm[31:2] == {12'b0, pred_tgt}); about 3-4 LUT levels,
  well before the bypass -> comparator branch cond arrives.
- bad = pt && !squash && !is_jalr && !((br_ok || jal) && match).
  This is a predicted-taken word that is not a direct branch/JAL to that
  exact target. It never happens in CoreMark, but formal's symbolic imem
  produces it.
- redirect = !squash && (jal_ok || jalr_ok || (br_ok && cond') || bad).
  bad is early, so it goes into the early LUT and the last LUT still
  takes cond / jalr_sum[1].
- redirect_target = is_jalr ? jalr_sum
                  : (bad ? pc : (pt ? pc4 : pc_imm)).
  The inner 3:1 mux is flops plus the early bad signal, and is_jalr stays
  the only select on the late jalr_sum input.
- On bad, replay: the word is killed like a squashed one (EX/MEM valid,
  reg_write, mem_read, mem_write cleared; divider start gated), the PC is
  redirected to the word's own pc, and valid[idx(pc)] is cleared on the
  same edge (unregistered clear, which beats any pending allocate). The
  refetch therefore misses and takes the normal path. This keeps
  liveness, rvfi_order and pc_fwd exact.
- BTB training is registered (upd_en/idx/data flops, written the next
  cycle), and only on !stall && valid && !squash && !bad:
  a hit branch updates its 2-bit counter (from the carried ctr); a
  missed taken aligned branch allocates with ctr = 2'b10; a missed
  aligned JAL allocates with ctr = 2'b11. JALR is never installed.
  Not-taken misses write nothing.
- pc_next / branch_taken for RVFI keep their current logic, which
  already derives them from cond.

Expected: cycles 4.528M -> about 4.26M (-5.5 to -6.5%). r1s2 measured
-6.6% with an unlimited-capacity predecode predictor, and a 32-entry
exact-tag BTB loses a little to cold misses and conflicts. Fmax should
stay within about 1-2% of 108.66 MHz, because the redirect cone is the
same depth and the new IF path starts at a flop. Net about +4 to +7%.
If the trace shows many conflict misses, the implementer may go to 64
entries (pc[7:2], tag pc[14:8]). Check `make timing` to confirm that
no u_if/btb path is in the top 5.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r6s2 (regression, -12.01%): A PC-indexed 32-entry LUT-RAM BTB on r5s1 was argued to be Fmax-neutral because every new path starts at a flop: the lookup runs from the PC flop in parallel with the imem read, pt picks target or pc+4 with redirect as the last select, the prediction is checked in EX from ID/EX flops with replay-and-invalidate on `bad`, and training is registered; but 211.16 means Fmax fell to ~95.6 MHz even if cycles did not change (~90 MHz if they fell to the predicted ~4.26M), against the champion's 108.66, a loss of at least 12%, nearly twice the ~6.6% cycle cut any predictor can deliver here; likely costs that the LUT-level estimate missed are the extra loads on the PC nets (the PC is also io_imemAddr, the head of the imem -> ID decode path), the two-bank LUT-RAM read mux, tag/valid compare and ~30-bit pt fanout into the PC D-mux, and the implementer's rewrite of the EX redirect as a 6-mask eq/!eq/lt/!lt/ltu/!ltu SOP plus the `taken = branch_cond ^ pt` training logic, both adding loads on the already-critical compare outputs; this is the sixth predictor port to lose and the second case after r6s0 where a "flops-only, same depth" LUT-count argument failed badly near 9.2 ns, so do not queue another predictor variant until `make timing` on the real diff, across the scored seeds, shows that no u_if/btb, u_if/pc or EX redirect path has moved up.

title: IF skid register: bank the fetch word during back-end stalls so a later imem stall costs no bubble
motivation:
The ~22% random imem stall is now the largest single source of lost
cycles. At ~4.53M cycles for ~3.2M instructions, every cycle in which
ID could accept a word but io_imemReady = 0 is a bubble: roughly
0.22 x (cycles not stalled by the back end), about 19% of all cycles.
Today the fetch is thrown away whenever the back end stalls (load-use
/ MUL-use bubble, dmem stall, divide): the PC holds and the same word
must be fetched again, and if the bus is not ready on the resume
cycle, a second bubble follows. About 45-50k back-end stall episodes
per CoreMark iteration are wasted fetch slots. The last six timing-only
trims and predictor ports all lost to seed noise; this move saves
cycles instead, and every path it adds starts at a flop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a one-entry skid register (buf_valid, buf_instr[31:0], buf_pc[31:2])
in if_stage. On a cycle where the back end stalls (load_use ||
dmem_stall || div_busy), the buffer is empty, imem is ready and there
is no redirect, capture the fetch word and its pc and advance the PC.
While the buffer is full, ID decodes buf_instr / buf_pc instead of
io_imemData / pc, and on every cycle ID accepts the word, IF refills
the buffer from the bus when ready (PC advances), or empties it when
not ready (PC holds). A full buffer is one banked word, so the next
imem stall is hidden (ID still gets a valid word) instead of costing a
bubble. A redirect clears buf_valid and loads the target as it does
now; the word ID sees on the redirect cycle is still captured with
squash = 1 and killed in EX, so branch cost is unchanged.
PC update: pc <= redirect ? target : (imem_ready && !(buf_valid &&
backend_stall)) ? pc + 4 : pc. The ID word valid is buf_valid ||
imem_ready. The back-end stall terms and their priorities in
hazard_unit are unchanged; only imem_stall leaves stall_if/flush_if
and becomes "no word for ID" = !buf_valid && !imem_ready.
Estimate: ~50k stall episodes/iteration, ~80% of them see a ready bus
cycle with an empty buffer, and ~55-65% of the banked words meet an
imem stall before the next taken branch flushes them, which saves
~20-25k cycles per iteration, 4-6% of cycles. Fmax risk is one LUT
level (a 2:1 mux on a flop select buf_valid) at the head of the ID
decode / regfile-address / load-use compare paths; in the timed
netlist io_imemData is an LFSR flop, and `make timing` on the champion
(placement 0, 103.6 MHz) shows that all top-25 setup paths are EX paths
(EX/MEM.alu_result -> bypass -> compare chain -> redirect -> PC CE/D
at 9.58-9.62 ns, plus one shifter and one DSP->xres path); no ID, IF
or hazard path is in the list, so ID should absorb the extra level.
Rules to keep the champion's critical path unchanged: redirect stays
the last term into the PC CE (CE = redirect | pc_advance, with
pc_advance = imem_ready & !(buf_valid & backend_stall) built only from
flops and the existing stall terms) and the PC D mux stays
redirect ? target : pc + 4; buf_valid's next state may use redirect,
but nothing in EX reads the buffer. In the late dmem -> load-align ->
mem_result -> ID/EX forward path (r6s0's worst path once the EX tails
were cut), the muxed word only feeds the forward select and the
const-operand select, which arrive well before the BSRAM data, and the
mem_result select must stay last in front of each ID/EX flop.
One entry is enough: most back-end stall episodes (load-use, MUL-use,
dmem stall) last one cycle, and a full buffer keeps itself full with
one refill per accepted word until an imem stall uses it up.

changes.description: Add buf_valid / buf_instr / buf_pc flops. Buffer: if empty, capture {imem_data, pc} when imem_ready && backend_stall && !redirect; if full and ID accepts (!backend_stall), refill from bus when ready else clear; if full and back end stalled, hold. Reset clears buf_valid.

Split out backend_stall = load_use || dmem_stall || div_busy (exported to IF); flush_if/stall_if no longer take imem_stall directly (IF owns PC-advance). lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260929-001-r7s0 (regression, -8.83%): A one-entry IF skid buffer (buf_valid/buf_instr/buf_pc) that banks the fetch word during load-use, dmem and divide stalls, so that a later ~22% imem stall costs no bubble, scored 218.79 against the ~240 champion, so Fmax fell to ~99 MHz even if cycles did not change, or ~93–95 MHz if they fell by the estimated 4–6%, against 108.66 MHz, a loss larger than any cycle saving the buffer can give; the likely cause is that the `buf_valid ? buf_instr : io_imemData` mux sits in front of every consumer of the fetch word at once (ID decode, the LUT-RAM regfile read addresses and the hazard unit's rs compare, which undoes r2s0's raw-imem_data rs cut), so the imem word -> mux -> rs==rd compare -> load_use -> backend_stall -> pc_advance -> PC CE/io_imemAddr loop gained a level plus 63 new buffer-CE loads on backend_stall, and the "placement-0 top-25 has no ID/IF path, so ID has slack" argument failed the same way the "flops only, same depth" arguments did in r6s0 and r6s2; a fetch-side IPC move worth ≤6% must keep the hazard and PC-enable cone reading raw imem_data (for example, compare the banked word's rs fields in the capture cycle and select only the registered hit bit by buf_valid) and be checked with `make timing` across the scored seeds before it is queued.

title: Decoupled fetch: 1-entry IF skid buffer that keeps fetching during backend stalls and hides later imem stalls (no extra redirect bubble)
motivation:
Timing on the r5s1 champion (108.66 MHz, 4.53M cycles) is saturated:
r6s0 measured four families tied within 0.04 ns on placement 0 (branch
compare -> redirect -> PC, DSP tail, shifter tail, and dmem BSRAM ->
load align -> ID forward -> ID/EX op). r6s0 (-3.4%) and r6s1 (-7.0%)
show that further LUT trimming, or moving the bypass, loses to routing
and to the ~5% spread between seeds. Six predictor ports have lost
because their IF logic landed on the PC/redirect paths. Cycle count, by
contrast, is exact: any cycle removed without adding a new path near
9.2 ns counts in full.

The largest cycle loss that no one has tried to cut is imem
backpressure. bench_stall_gen draws imem_ready independently every
cycle (xorshift, ~22% not-ready) whether or not the core fetches. With
IF/ID purely combinational, every not-ready cycle becomes an ID/EX
bubble. That is about 0.22 x ~4.1M front-end-active cycles, roughly
0.9M cycles or ~20% of the run. Meanwhile, on every backend stall cycle
(dmem stall ~0.28 cycles per memory op, load-use and MUL-use
interlocks, DIV) stall_if holds the PC. The imem word delivered on
those cycles (78% of them are ready) is thrown away and must be fetched
again later, when it can hit an imem stall. That is roughly 400-550k
backend-stall cycles of wasted fetch bandwidth, which a decoupled
front end can bank.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 1-entry fetch skid buffer (fb_valid, fb_instr, fb_pc) between the
imem port and ID, so the front end is decoupled from backend stalls by
one instruction:

  ID word    : instr = fb_valid ? fb_instr : io_imemData
               pc    = fb_valid ? fb_pc    : pc
               valid = fb_valid || imem_ready
  consume    = ID/EX captures a real word this cycle
               = !(load_use || dmem_stall || div_busy)
  PC advance = redirect ? target
             : (imem_ready && (!fb_valid || consume)) ? pc + 4 : pc
  buffer     : redirect                           -> fb_valid <= 0
               !fb_valid & !consume & imem_ready  -> fb <= {imem word, pc}
               fb_valid  &  consume & imem_ready  -> fb <= {imem word, pc}
               fb_valid  &  consume & !imem_ready -> fb_valid <= 0 (stall hidden)
               fb_valid  & !consume               -> hold

When the backend stalls with the buffer empty and imem ready, the
delivered word (the one ID could not take) is parked and the PC moves
ahead. From then on ID decodes from the buffer while imem refills it
each cycle. The next imem not-ready cycle drains the buffer instead of
inserting a bubble. A redirect flushes the buffer, so with the buffer
empty ID reads imem directly, and a taken branch still costs exactly 1
bubble. The squash_q wrong-path kill is unchanged: the word in ID
during the redirect cycle, from either source, is captured with
squash = 1. Load-use and every other ID-side rule see the muxed word.
The parked word is re-decoded next cycle against the updated
EX/MEM / MEM/WB state, so the operand forwarding and the write-first
bypass need no change.

Estimated gain: about 400-550k backend-stall cycles, 78% of them with
imem ready, and each fill is kept only while the buffer is empty. A
fill hides one later imem stall if an imem stall arrives before the
next taken redirect (P ~ 0.6, with ~5-7 cycles between redirects and
22% stalls per cycle). That puts the cut at roughly 180-260k cycles, or
4-6% of 4.53M. The saving is exact and does not depend on the seed.

Timing discipline, so this does not repeat r6s0/r6s2:
  - The only new logic on an existing path is one LUT3 2:1 mux per
    instruction bit at the ID head (select fb_valid is a flop). The
    EX families (branch -> PC, DSP, shifter, ALU) and the dmem ->
    ID-forward path gain no loads and no levels. fb_valid is
    duplicated (for example a separate copy for the rs1/rs2 fields
    feeding the LUT-RAM regfile and the load-use compare) so no single
    net carries the ~70-way fanout.
  - Redirect stays the last select into the PC D pin with its priority
    unchanged. The new advance term (imem_ready && (!fb_valid ||
    consume)) replaces !stall_if in the non-redirect leg, so the PC CE
    keeps its depth: consume is the existing !stall_id and fb_valid is
    a flop.
  - fb_pc is a registered copy of pc captured with fb_instr. There is
    no pc - 4 adder. pc_imm = in.pc + imm keeps its single adder.
  - The buffer data flops load either the imem word or nothing (a
    2:1 CE plus data, off flops and imem_ready), so the new flops sit
    after the BSRAM, not in front of any existing path.
If `make timing` shows the ID head (imem BSRAM -> mux -> LUT-RAM read
-> bypass -> forward -> ID/EX op) above 9.2 ns, move the rs1/rs2
address mux ahead of the regfile read. Do this by giving the regfile a
second, registered read-address path fed from fb_instr (rs fields
registered alongside it), so the LUT-RAM address is either raw
imem_data or a flop and the mux falls after the RAM output, or by
precomputing the fb-side load-use compare from the registered rs
fields.

title: One-cycle-ahead BTB keyed by the predecessor PC: prediction registered before it is used, so no BTB logic sits in front of the PC and EX redirect depth is unchanged
motivation:
The predictors tried so far saved the expected cycles and then lost on Fmax.
r6s2 (PC-indexed 32-entry BTB) cut cycles from 4.528M to 4.238M (-6.4%) but
fell to 89.5 MHz. r5s2 (IF predecode) cut cycles 6.6% and fell to 92.4 MHz.
The champion r5s1 is at 108.66 MHz. Its worst path is
EX/MEM.alu_result -> 1-ahead bypass -> branch compare -> redirect -> PC
(u_ex -> u_if, 37 cells). r6s2's worst path ended at ID/EX.late through
`!redirect`, which means its rewritten 6-mask redirect SOP made that same
cone longer. Every earlier design put new logic on at least one of these:
  (a) the same-cycle IF path: PC or imem_data -> lookup/predecode -> PC D
      and the imem BSRAM address;
  (b) the late EX redirect cone.
The ~6% cycle cut is only a net win if neither (a) nor (b) gets deeper.
Taken branches and JALs are still the largest source of avoidable cycles:
each costs one squash bubble, ~290k cycles in total, ~6.4% of 4.53M.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a BTB that is read one fetch ahead. Every predictor output is a flop
by the time it reaches the PC mux. Verification is precomputed in ID, so
the EX redirect keeps today's one-mux-after-compare structure.

1. Lookup keyed by the predecessor (if_stage.sv). Each cycle, index a
   32-entry LUT-RAM table (async read, like the regfile) with the PC flop.
   Entry = {valid, 6-bit partial tag, 2-bit counter, off[20:1]}.
   Entry[p] means "the word at p+4 is a branch/JAL with offset `off`".
   The lookup computes:
     ehit = valid && tag match
     hit  = ehit && ctr[1]
     pred = (pc+4) + sext(off)   (one adder, off the next_pc path)
   The result is registered with exactly the PC's enable:
     if (redirect)      hit_q <= 0
     else if (!stall) { hit_q <= hit && !hit_q; pred_q <= pred;
                        ehit_q, ctr_q, off_q <= lookup }
   Clearing hit_q on a redirect or a taken prediction means only
   sequentially reached words are predicted.
   Next PC becomes:
     redirect ? redirect_target : (hit_q ? pred_q : pc+4)
   with the CE unchanged. The inner mux is flops/adder-only. redirect and
   redirect_target stay the last select, so the late path through the PC
   D input and the imem BSRAM address is the same depth as today. The PC
   flop gains only the index/tag and adder loads. No LUT-RAM read, tag
   compare or adder sits between any flop and the PC D input in the same
   cycle, unlike r6s2 and r5s2.
   IF/ID carries pt (= hit_q), ehit, ctr and off with the word.

2. ID-side verification, registered (id_stage.sv).
     pv = pt && valid && ((is_branch || is_jal) && imm == sext(off_q))
   Compare the imm_gen output (or the raw B/J imm bits plus opcode) with
   off_q. That is XOR + a 3-level AND tree after imem_data, shorter than
   the existing imem -> regfile read -> forward -> operand-mux ID paths.
   A verified hit means the word already fetched after this one is
   exactly pc+imm, the correct target. This holds under formal's
   arbitrary instruction stream because the check is against the actual
   fetched bits, so a tag is only a filter against false hits.
   Register these in ID/EX:
     alt_tgt = !pt ? pc_imm : ((!pv && is_ctl) ? pc : pc+4)
               pc_imm is the late adder, so it goes into the last select.
     replay  = pt && !pv && (is_branch || is_jump)
               A mismatched control op is refetched unpredicted.
     force   = (pt && !pv) || (jal_ok && !pv)
     t_sel / n_sel = redirect-if-taken (br_ok && !pv) and
               redirect-if-not-taken (is_branch && pv), pre-swapped by
               cmp_inv.
     sel_jalr = is_jalr && !pt
   Keep pc_imm in ID/EX for RVFI pc_next only; synthesis prunes it.

3. EX redirect (ex_stage.sv), with the same LUT structure as today:
     raw      = sel_eq&eq | sel_lt&lt | sel_ltu&ltu
     redirect = !squash && (force || (sel_jalr && jalr_ok) ||
                            (raw ? t_sel : n_sel))
     redirect_target = sel_jalr ? jalr_sum : alt_tgt
   Today the cond term is br_ok && (cmp_inv ^ raw), also a 3-input
   function of raw. So branch_cond gains no LUT level, and nothing new
   loads the compare outputs. Do NOT write a per-mask SOP (the r6s2
   mistake). replay (a flop) also clears EX/MEM valid and reg_write, the
   same way squash does. Only control ops replay, so mem_*, div and late
   are unaffected.
   A repeated redirect during a dmem stall or div_busy re-targets the
   same PC. That is idempotent and is already how branches behave today.

4. Training, registered. For a non-squashed, non-replayed br_ok/jal_ok
   in EX, register:
     {we, idx/tag of (pc-4), off = imm[20:1], ctr_new}
   and write the LUT-RAM the next cycle.
     - Counter: if ehit, saturate ctr up/down by taken.
     - On a miss, allocate only when taken: ctr = 3 for JAL or a backward
       branch, 2 for a forward branch.
     - Never train on JALR; returns keep their one-bubble redirect.
   Every prediction is verified, so stale reads, aliasing and unreset
   contents are all harmless. Clear the contents only under the regfile's
   VERILATOR/RISCV_FORMAL/FORMAL ifdef, so cosim is deterministic and
   synthesis still gets LUT-RAM.

Expected result:
- Cycles: ~4.27-4.30M, i.e. -5 to -6%. Slightly below r6s2's -6.4%,
  because words reached by a redirect or a taken prediction are not
  predicted.
- Fmax: within ~1% of the champion if the redirect cone is left unchanged.
The implementer must run `make timing` on the real diff before handing
off. It passes only if:
- no new u_if/btb, pred_q or hit_q path appears near the top;
- the u_ex -> u_if and u_ex -> u_id(late/squash) arrivals are no worse
  than the champion's 14.95 ns.
If ID verification shows up, move the offset compare to the raw B/J imm
bits so it does not go through imm_gen.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260929-003-r7s2 (regression, +3.34%): The one-cycle-ahead BTB (32-entry LUT-RAM keyed by the predecessor PC, so hit_q/pred_q are already flops at the PC mux with redirect still the last select; the offset is verified in ID against the fetched word's imm and pre-resolved into registered frc / t_sel / n_sel / alt_tgt, so the EX redirect stays one LUT `raw ? t_sel : n_sel` after the compare; mispredicted control ops replay like squash; training is registered into entry[pc-4]) cut the predictor's Fmax cost from r6s2's ≥12% to roughly 2–3% (~105–106.6 MHz if cycles fell to the predicted 4.24–4.30M, against 108.66), which confirms that earlier ports lost to same-cycle lookup/predecode logic in front of the PC and to a wider redirect cone, not to prediction itself; it was rejected only by the 4.6% acceptance margin (needed ~251.0, got 248.01), and with a ≤6.6% cycle ceiling a ~5.5% cut clears that margin only if Fmax stays within ~1% (≥ ~107.4 MHz at 4.28M cycles), so do not redesign the predictor again; measure this diff's real cycles and `make timing` across the scored seeds (the implementer reported neither), find the new load that costs the last ~2 MHz (unmeasured candidates: index/tag/adder fanout on the PC flop that is also io_imemAddr, the ID offset-verify compare, the replay term on EX/MEM valid/reg_write), and either trim it or stack this front end with an orthogonal gain in one diff so the pair clears the margin.

title: Cut the heads of all four tied 14.49 ns path families (flop bypass selects, post-chain compare select, flat load forward)
motivation:
`make timing` on the r5s1 champion at the scored placement option 1
(108.658 MHz) shows a four-way tie within 0.04 ns (arrival 14.455-14.497):
  F1 dmem BSRAM -> load align -> mem_result -> ID/EX.op_b (6-8 cells)
  F2 EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write -> fwd select -> alu_b -> DSP -> EX/MEM.xres
  F3 EX/MEM.alu_result -> 1-ahead bypass -> branch compare -> redirect
     -> PC (26 cells; also -> ID/EX.squash)
  F4 EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write -> fwd -> ALU -> alu_result, and
     ID/EX.alu_sel.sub -> adder -> SLT -> alu_result[0] (36 cells)
LESSONS show cutting only some tied paths buys nothing (r2s0, r6s0) and
r6s0 lost exactly because it trimmed EX tails while F1 (dmem -> ID
op_b) stayed and became its worst path. F2/F3/F4 share one head: the
EX bypass mux whose select is `hit && EX/MEM.reg_write`, so a single
reg_write flop drives ~130 mux LUTs in front of every EX consumer.
This diff attacks the heads of all four families at zero cycle cost.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
No pipeline or cycle-count change (cycles stay 4,527,646); only the
first/last LUTs of the four tied families move.
(A) F2/F4 — fully qualified 1-ahead forward selects registered in ID.
hit = (ID/EX.rd == rs) && rd != 0 && ID/EX.ctrl.reg_write &&
!ID/EX.squash && !ID/EX.ctrl.is_jump && !ID/EX.late. This is exact:
a jump never needs a 1-ahead forward (aligned -> redirect squashes the
next word; misaligned -> trap, must not forward); LOAD/MUL*/DIV* are
`late` and always interlocked; bubbles and squashed words carry
reg_write = 0 or squash = 1; a DIV holds ID so its successor is
captured after the load-use bubble. EX's fwd_rs1/fwd_rs2/fwd_a/fwd_b
become plain flops (forward_unit passes them through); keep them as
separate flops per consumer (and split rs1/rs2 selects into two
16-bit-half copies with syn_preserve) so no select net drives more
than ~32 LUTs. EX/MEM.reg_write leaves the bypass cone entirely.
(B) F3 — branch compare with the bypass mux after the chains. EX
computes eq/lt/ltu for (alu_result_fwd, rs2_val), (rs1_val,
alu_result_fwd) and (rs1_val, rs2_val) in parallel from flops, and a
registered one-hot pair select (from the ID hits; both-hit implies
rs1 == rs2 so eq=1, lt=ltu=0) picks the three bits, folded with the
registered sel_eq/sel_lt/sel_ltu/cmp_inv into the go term. The
redirect becomes flop -> carry chain -> 1-2 LUTs -> PC mux, with no
32-bit mux and no 130-load select at its head. rs1/rs2 muxes remain
for the AGU, JALR, divider and store data only.
(C) F1 — flat load forward into ID. In EX, register one-hot load-lane
controls into EX/MEM (byte lane b0..b3, half lane h0/h1, word, sign
vs zero fill) so each load_data bit is one AND-OR level of dmem_rdata.
In ID, split the 2-ahead forward: fwd_ld (producer is a LOAD) and
fwd_nl (ALU / xres result) with the non-load value premuxed in
parallel with the BSRAM read, so every ID/EX operand flop sees
dmem_rdata -> lane AND-OR -> one LUT3 (fwd_ld ? load_data : rest).
mem_to_reg no longer sits between the BSRAM and the ID/EX flops.
(D) F4 tail — SLT/SLTU bit 0: take the sign/borrow from a separate
dedicated compare chain (same operands, a - b) so alu_sel.sub is not
also the adder-invert select on the 36-cell SLT path; or leave it if
(A) already removes the head.
Expected: every family loses one LUT level plus a heavily loaded
route (~0.6-1.0 ns of 9.2 ns), so scored Fmax ~113-117 MHz at
unchanged cycles (+4-8%). Implementer must run
`python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options --paths 25` on the
real diff and check that no family remains at the old arrival.

title: Retime the fetch-address mux past the PC register (redirect drives 2 flops, not 32 PC CE/D pins) and take the DSP off the 1-ahead bypass (MUL reads ID/EX flops, 1-ahead MUL dependency joins the late interlock)
motivation:
Champion r5s1 is 108.66 MHz (seeds 103.6 / 108.66 / 108.66) at 4.53M
cycles. Its logged worst path is family A (37 cells):
EX/MEM.alu_result -> rs1 1-ahead bypass LUT -> 32-cell compare chain
-> 3 LUTs (cond select, br_ok & cond, jal/jalr OR, squash) ->
redirect (fanout 33) -> 0.68 ns route -> PC clock-enable LUT
(CE = redirect | !stall, fanout 30) -> 0.80 ns route -> pc_*/CE.
Paths from the same bypass head tie with it within 0.04 ns. Family B
goes alu_a bypass -> sign-extension LUT -> 1.09 ns route -> DSP
(3.76 ns) -> 2 LUTs -> xres. Family C goes alu_a bypass -> barrel
shifter -> AND-OR -> alu_result.
Lessons r6s0, r6s1 and r7s0 each tried to shave LUTs from these tails
or relocate the bypass mux, and each one lost Fmax: the extra operand
copies and bypass loads cost routing that LUT counting does not see.
Lesson r5s1 is the counter-example. It won by moving work across a
register boundary, with a cheap 1-cycle interlock paying for it.
Two of the tied families are not required to sit in the 1-cycle
ALU -> bypass -> ALU recurrence at all:
  - The PC CE/D pins are the tail of A only because the redirect mux
    sits in front of the PC register. The fetch address can equally
    well be selected after the register, from flops. The FPGA bench
    drives imem data from an LFSR and only XORs io_imemAddr into an
    LED, so a flop -> 1 LUT fetch address is free.

    source was produced by the immediately preceding non-late
    instruction. A LOAD -> MUL pair (matrix_mul_*: lh; mul) is
    already interlocked by `late`, and after the bubble ID forwards

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two structural moves in one diff, keeping cycles within about +0.3%.

1. Fetch-address mux moved after the PC register (cuts family A's
   tail by about 1.2-1.5 ns). In if_stage, replace the single
   `pc` register (redirect ? target : !stall ? pc+4 : pc, with CE)
   with three CE-free registers:
     pc_seq  : sequential fetch address
     tgt_q   : redirect target, captured EVERY cycle (no CE, no
               redirect in its cone): tgt_q <= redirect_target
               (= is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],0} : ID/EX.pc_imm)
     take_q  : take_q <= redirect   (reset 0)
   and a combinational fetch address off flops:
     cur_pc      = take_q ? tgt_q : pc_seq;     // one LUT3 per bit
     io_imemAddr = cur_pc;  out.pc = cur_pc;
     pc_seq     <= reset ? RESET_PC : (stall ? cur_pc : cur_pc + 4);
   The +4 adder runs off flops in parallel with the load-use cone, and
   stall is the last 2:1 select (LUT3 per bit, no CE). Do not put
   stall into the carry-in: the LFSR -> rs==rd -> load_use -> stall
   cone plus a 30-bit ripple would become a new long path.
   This fetches the same address every cycle as today. With a
   redirect, the next cur_pc is the target. It still overrides a
   stall, because take_q is set regardless of stall and pc_seq's
   value is ignored that cycle. With a stall and no redirect, pc_seq
   captures cur_pc (which may be the target from the previous
   redirect), so the fetch holds. A branch held in EX by a dmem
   stall re-fires redirect every cycle, which is idempotent (take_q=1,
   tgt_q=same target). ID/EX.squash still captures redirect when ID
   advances, exactly as today. The redirect then fans out to just
   two D pins, take_q and ID/EX.squash, instead of 32 PC D-mux LUTs
   plus the CE LUT. That removes the CE LUT and its fanout-30 route
   and the fanout-33 redirect route from family A. The cost is
   one LUT3 (take_q mux) at the head of the pc+4 adder, the ID
   pc+imm adder and ID/EX.pc. All three start at flops and are far
   from critical: the pc_imm adder is dominated by imm from the
   LFSR -> imm_gen. Add a syn_keep'd duplicate of take_q if its
   fanout (~64: the cur_pc mux) shows up. While in EX, also
   precombine the flop-only redirect terms, so that after the
   compare chain redirect is at most LUT(cond) + one LUT:
     go_j = !squash & jal_ok (flops); go_b = !squash & br_ok (flops)
     redirect = go_j | jalr_ok_nosq | (go_b & cond)
   This keeps the misalign / reg_write semantics unchanged.

2. DSP off the 1-ahead bypass (cuts family B and ~66 bypass loads).
   alu_core gets separate multiplier operand ports. In ex_stage, the
   DSP reads the ID/EX flops directly:
     prod = $signed({mul_sa & op_a[31], op_a}) *
            $signed({mul_sb & op_b[31], op_b})
   where op_a/op_b are in.op_a / in.op_b, never alu_a/alu_b. For MUL*
   both operands are registers, so op_a/op_b already carry the
   regfile write-first (3-ahead) and ID mem_result (2-ahead) forwards.
   The sign bits are a LUT2 off flops beside the DSP input, not
   behind the bypass. The ALTOPS stand-ins use the same op_a/op_b.
   The only case the bypass covered, a MUL whose rs1/rs2 was written
   by the instruction directly ahead, becomes a 1-cycle interlock
   through the existing load-use compare in hazard_unit:
     hit      = (id_ex_rd == if_rs1 || id_ex_rd == if_rs2) && id_ex_rd != 0
     load_use = hit && (id_ex_late || id_is_mul_raw)
   id_is_mul_raw = io_imemData[6:0]==7'b0110011 &&
   [31:25]==7'b0000001 && ![14] is decoded from the raw fetch word in
   parallel with the rd==rs compare. That is 2 LUT levels in
   parallel, so the final hit & (late|mul) LUT is no deeper than
   today's. A spurious stall (the producer in ID/EX is a store/branch
   whose rd field is imm bits, or a squashed word) is correct and
   rare; to avoid even that, register an ID/EX `wr` bit and use
   id_ex_late | (id_ex_wr & mul). After the bubble the producer is
   in EX/MEM, and ID forwards it through mem_result into op_a/op_b as
   for any 2-ahead source. xres stays in EX/MEM behind the MEM late
   select (r5s1), and the MUL-use interlock via `late` is unchanged.
   CoreMark MULs are fed by loads (already interlocked) or by
   long-lived index registers, so the added cycles should be well
   under 0.3%.

3. Conditional, only if `make timing` after 1+2 shows the shifter
   family (C) or dmem -> load-align -> ID/EX (the path r6s0/r6s1
   exposed at ~105 MHz) as the only remaining path above 8.8 ns on
   the scored seeds: do not trim LUTs. Report it in the notes so the
   next round can move that work across a boundary. Do not add
   operand copies to the bypass nets (lesson r6s0).

Expected: family A loses about 1.2-1.5 ns (CE LUT, two high-fanout
routes, one LUT), and family B loses about 2 ns (bypass LUT,
sign-extension LUT, two routes). Family C and the dmem -> ID path
gain a little from lighter alu_a/alu_b and redirect nets. If C
and dmem -> ID sit at about 8.8-9.0 ns on the better seeds, Fmax is
~111-116 MHz at ~4.535M cycles, which gives fitness ~245-256
(+2-7%). The PC move alone is zero-cycle and cannot hurt IPC. It is
also a prerequisite for re-stacking r7s2's one-cycle-ahead BTB,
whose worst path again ended at u_if/pc.

title: Re-land r7s2's one-cycle-ahead BTB with redirect taken off every predictor flop enable and off the EX/MEM kill LUT
motivation:
r7s2 (one-cycle-ahead BTB keyed by the predecessor PC) is the only predictor
that came close. Its measured numbers (log.jsonl): cycles 4,241,128 (-6.33%
vs the champion's 4,527,646), median-seed Fmax 105.18 MHz (-3.2% vs 108.66),
LUT4 2205 -> 2520. That scored +3.34%, short of the 4.6% margin.
Its worst path is the champion's own EX redirect cone
(ID/EX.rs2_hit_ex -> 1-ahead bypass -> compare -> redirect -> u_if/pc), but
it arrives 0.55 ns later (15.50 vs 14.95 ns). The number of LUT levels in the
cone did not change, so the extra delay is almost certainly load and
placement on the redirect net:
  - in r7s2 the payload flops pred_q[31:0], off_q[19:0], ctr_q, ehit_q were
    written under `if (redirect) hit_q<=0; else if (!stall) {...}`, which
    gives about 57 flops a CE of !redirect && !stall, so redirect drives
    a CE LUT and a large new flop group next to the PC;
  - `replay` was added as a separate input next to squash on EX/MEM
    valid/reg_write.
ISS count of the timed CoreMark region (2,922,016 instructions): 529,588
branches (294,425 taken), 49,367 JAL, 13,735 JALR (all returns, no indirect
calls). Taken branches + JAL are ~344k redirect bubbles, and r7s2 already
removed 287k of them. Returns are only 0.3% of cycles, so return prediction
is not worth any Fmax. The IPC side is solved; the whole remaining gap is
the ~3% Fmax loss.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-implement r7s2 as specified in log.jsonl, keeping its IPC design as is:
a 32-entry LUT-RAM where entry[p] predicts the word at p+4 ({valid, 6-bit
tag, 2-bit ctr, off[20:1]}); hit_q/pred_q registered with the PC enable;
next PC = redirect ? redirect_target : (hit_q ? pred_q : pc+4) with redirect
as the last select; the offset verified in ID against the fetched word's
imm (raw B/J imm bits, not through imm_gen); frc / t_sel / n_sel / alt_tgt /
sel_jalr registered in ID/EX so EX redirect = !squash && (frc ||
sel_jalr&&jalr_ok || (raw ? t_sel : n_sel)) (NOT a per-mask SOP); replay
on mismatched control ops; registered training into entry[pc-4];
allocate-on-taken; no JALR training. Then change only the loads that
r7s2 added to the redirect net:

  1. Redirect touches one predictor flop only. hit_q is the only flop
     cleared by redirect (hit_q <= redirect ? 0 : (!stall ? hit && !hit_q
     : hit_q)). pred_q/off_q/ctr_q/ehit_q enable on !stall_if alone. This
     is safe: when redirect fires, hit_q is 0 on the next cycle, so
     whatever the payload captured is don't-care, and the payload is
     re-captured on the next PC advance before hit_q can be 1 again. The
     PC flop CE (redirect || !stall) is unchanged, so the redirect net
     returns to the champion's loads (PC D mux + PC CE + squash) plus one
     hit_q LUT.
  2. One kill flop instead of squash + replay on the EX/MEM LUTs. In ID/EX
     register kill <= redirect || replay_d (replay_d is registered from ID
     flops and imem-side logic, not from EX). EX/MEM valid / reg_write /
     mem_read / mem_write / divider start / training / late use !kill
     exactly where the champion uses !squash, so those LUTs keep the
     champion's input count. The redirect term still uses !squash (the
     replayed op must fire its own frc redirect to alt_tgt = pc).
  3. Do not add loads on the EX compare outputs, rs1/rs2 or
     redirect_target beyond r7s2's `raw ? t_sel : n_sel` and
     `sel_jalr ? jalr_sum : alt_tgt`. Training registers
     {branch_taken, pc, imm} from the EX/MEM-captured values (EX/MEM
     already holds branch_taken, pc and branch_target; take off from
     instr bits in EX/MEM) and derives idx/tag/ctr_new one cycle
     later, so the training datapath hangs off EX/MEM flops, not off
     the EX compare.
  4. Put the BTB index/tag reads on pc[6:2] / pc[12:7] straight from the
     PC flop. Keep the pc+4+sext(off) adder in the payload D path only.
     Keep the LUT-RAM clear under the regfile's VERILATOR / RISCV_FORMAL /
     FORMAL ifdef so synthesis still gets LUT-RAM.

Expected: cycles ~4.24M (-6.3%, measured on r7s2; training from EX/MEM
instead of EX delays the table update by one cycle, which is at most a
few hundred cycles). If Fmax returns to within ~1.5% of 108.66
(>= ~107 MHz), fitness is ~250-253 (+4.5-5.5%). Before handing off,
the implementer must run `make timing` and check that the top paths
are the champion's families (alu_result/rs?_hit_ex -> u_if/pc,
dmem -> u_id op_b) with arrival <= ~15.0 ns, and that no u_if hit_q/pred_q,
BTB LUT-RAM or ID verify path is in the top 10. If the redirect -> PC
path is still the worst and longer than 14.95 ns, check the P&R report
for redirect fanout and duplicate the redirect LUT (one copy for the
PC D mux, one for squash/kill/hit_q) with syn_keep.

title: Absorb the MUL product into the DSP output register and move the DIV/MUL xres select to MEM
motivation:
Measured with `make timing` (placement option 0) during hypothesis
generation. On the r5s1 champion (103.6 MHz), all top-25 paths start at
EX/MEM.alu_result, and the first hop is a 1.43 ns route to the bypass
LUT. They form three tied families within 0.04 ns: bypass -> compare
chain -> redirect -> PC CE; bypass -> DSP -> xres; and the ALU loop. A

bypass (+64 FF). The alu_result head disappeared, but option 0 fell to
102.8 MHz. The new top paths are ID/EX.op_b_31 -> DSP -> EX/MEM.xres

floor, not the heads. Of the three bodies, the DSP path has the least

title: Decoupled front end: registered 2-bank 1K-word BSRAM fetch store feeds IF on imem stalls (all new fetch signals are flops)
motivation:
Every EX/ID timing diff since r5s1 has landed at 105-108 MHz (seed noise
is about 5%), and the eight predictor builds each cut at most ~6.6% of
cycles and then lost Fmax. The largest cycle bucket nobody has touched is
the fetch bus itself. io_imemReady is an independent 100/128 per-cycle
draw (bench_stall_gen / main.cpp bus_accepts_main), so a core that must
take every word from the bus can never fetch more than 0.78 words/cycle.
Measured with a trace-driven cycle model: the ISS trace between the
CoreMark markers is 2,922,015 instructions. Replaying the champion's
hazard rules (1-bubble redirect, load/MUL/DIV-use interlock, 34-cycle
divide, dmem freeze) against the exact xorshift ready sequence gives
4,527,441 cycles, against the 4,527,646 measured for r5s1 (205-cycle
error). 817,203 of those cycles (18%) are imem-stall bubbles. The r7
skid buffers could only reach the ~150k that overlap back-end stalls.
To break the 0.78 cap, the front end needs its own instruction store.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small instruction store to IF that serves the fetch whenever
io_imemReady=0 and the word is resident. It is built so that every signal
it adds to the existing ID / hazard / PC cones comes straight from a flop,
which r7s0/r7s1 showed matters: in the timed wrapper io_imemData is an
LFSR flop, so a raw BSRAM read in front of decode would be slower than
what it replaces.

Store: two banks, EVEN (pc[2]=0) and ODD (pc[2]=1), each 512 x {valid,
tag = pc[19:12], word[31:0]} (41 bits), inferred as sync-read simple-
dual-port block RAMs (4 BSRAMs in total; the device has 46), so it holds
1K words / 4 KB.
  * Fill: in every cycle with imem_ready=1 and pc[31:20]==0, write
    {1, pc[19:12], io_imemData} to bank[pc[2]][pc[11:3]]. The write
    address is the PC flop, the data is the imem flop and WE is the ready
    flop, so there is no fill FSM, no refill stall and no bus change.
    Wrong-path words are real code, so they are filled too.
  * Read one cycle early, both sequential candidates at once: at the end
    of cycle t-2 the banks register the indexes of A and A+4 (one per
    bank, because they always differ in bit 2). Here A = stall_if ? pc :
    pc+4 is the next PC without the redirect term, so the EX compare ->
    redirect -> PC path gets no new loads. The expected tags (and
    A < 1 MB) are registered alongside.
  * In cycle t-1, after BSRAM clk-to-out, each bank compares valid and
    tag against its registered expected tag in parallel. The two words
    and hit bits are then selected with sel = pc[2] ^ !stall_if (held
    word vs next word) into fword_q[31:0] and hit_q.
  * Use in cycle t: fetch_ok = imem_ready || (hit_q && !red1_q &&
    !red2_q), where red1_q/red2_q are redirect delayed by 1 and 2 cycles.
    This is one LUT4 of flops, and the only new redirect load is the
    red1_q D pin. It replaces !imem_stall in hazard_unit (stall_if /
    flush_if) and IF valid. The ID word is imem_ready ? io_imemData :
    fword_q, a LUT3 whose inputs are all flops. The hazard unit's
    load-use compare keeps reading raw fields: compare id_ex_rd against
    io_imemData[19:15]/[24:20] and fword_q[19:15]/[24:20] in parallel,
    then pick the 1-bit hit by imem_ready.
  * Read/write collision: the only case is stall_if && fill in the same
    cycle (A == pc). Register coll_q and cancel that held-candidate hit,
    so the result does not depend on Gowin SDP collision semantics, and
    Verilator and hardware agree.
  * Reset: under VERILATOR / RISCV_FORMAL / FORMAL, clear the valid bits
    behaviorally on reset (the same pattern as reg_file.sv), so formal
    exercises the hit path inside its 20-step depth. The synthesis build
    runs a 512-cycle post-reset sweep that writes valid=0 and blocks
    fills and hits. The pipeline keeps running from the bus meanwhile,
    and the sweep ends long before the start_time marker.
Formal needs no contract change. checks_si.cfg has no imem-consistency
check, imem is symbolic, and whatever word the core decodes is reported
as rvfi_insn and checked as usual. Liveness can only improve, because a
hit only adds fetch opportunities. main.cpp still sees io_imemAddr = pc
every cycle, so the oob check is unchanged.

Modeled cycles for this exact design (hits unusable for the 2 cycles
after a redirect, a fill visible 2 cycles later): 3.863M for 1K words
(-14.7%, +17.2% fitness at unchanged Fmax). For comparison: 3.878M at
512 words, 3.899M at 256 words, and 3.719M if the index took the
redirect too; that variant is rejected because it puts BSRAM address
pins on the critical redirect net. New logic on existing paths: one LUT3
on the ID fetch word, one extra input on fetch_ok, and about 50 new
loads on stall_if/adv (bank index select, fword select). The last one
may need a replicated stall_if copy. The acceptance bar (+4.6%) holds
down to ~97.4 MHz (-10%), so the expected range is +11..+17%.

title: Predecessor-keyed BTB plus a registered branch-mispredict redirect, so the 32-bit compare chain no longer reaches the PC
motivation:
r7s2's one-cycle-ahead BTB (keyed by the predecessor PC) cut cycles from
~4.528M to 4,241,128 (-6.3%). That is almost the whole taken-redirect
ceiling, and it would have cleared the 4.6% margin at any Fmax >= ~106.5 MHz.
It scored 248.01 only because its median Fmax fell to 105.18 MHz. Its
logged worst path was ID/EX.rs2_hit_ex -> bypass -> branch compare chain
-> redirect -> u_if/pc (9 cells). That is the same compare -> redirect ->
PC family that r8s0 measured as one of the champion's two tied families.
The BTB added a third PC source and a wider redirect cone on exactly that
path. The other predictor builds ran into the same thing: a zero-bubble
predictor forces the branch outcome, the predicted target and the
high-fanout PC select into one cycle. A predictor that works here must
keep the PC D-input fed only from flops and short cones.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep r7s2's front end: a 32-entry predecessor-keyed LUT-RAM BTB (valid,
tag, 2-bit counter, branch/JAL offset). Its prediction is registered
(hit_q / pred_q) before it reaches the PC. On top of it, make the
conditional-branch mispredict redirect registered.
  - The EX branch compare now drives only single flops: br_redir_q,
    br_tgt_q and the ID/EX squash/late D-inputs. It no longer drives the
    32-bit PC select.
  - The combinational EX redirect keeps only terms that are flops or
    short: a non-predicted or wrongly predicted JAL (jal_ok && !pv), JALR
    (unchanged from the champion), and a false BTB hit on a non-control
    instruction (frc flop, redirect to pc+4).
  - PC D = br_redir_q ? br_tgt_q : redirect_c ? target_c
           : stall ? pc : (hit_q ? pred_q : pc+4).
Cycle model:
  - A correctly predicted taken branch or JAL: 0 bubbles (it was 1).
  - A mispredicted conditional branch: 2 bubbles (it was 1). The word
    behind it is squashed through the existing compare -> ID/EX.squash
    D-input. The next word is squashed by squash_d |= br_redir_q.
  - JAL misses, JALR and false hits: 1 bubble, as now.
Set br_redir_q only when EX/MEM advances (!stall_ex_mem). Then a branch
held in EX by a dmem stall redirects once, on release.
Estimate: r7s2 measured 4.241M cycles. The extra bubble per conditional
mispredict adds roughly 40-80k cycles (CoreMark crc/state branches are
data-dependent), giving about 4.28-4.32M (-4.6% to -5.5%).
The compare -> PC family is gone and the BTB feeds the PC only from
flops, so Fmax should return to the champion's range (~106-109 MHz). The
remaining limits are the DSP bypass path and the dmem -> ID forward.
Expected fitness: +3% to +8%.
Implement from r7s2's structure. Do not add LUTs beyond what the BTB
needs: no parallel compares, no duplicated operand copies. Before handing
off, run `make timing` across the scored seeds and confirm that no
u_ex -> u_if/pc path is near the top.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r9s2 (regression, -8.51%): Taking the branch compare off the PC on top of the predecessor-keyed BTB (a conditional mispredict now redirects one cycle later from br_redir_q/br_tgt_q and costs 2 bubbles, while JAL misses, JALR and false hits keep the 1-bubble combinational redirect) did not bring Fmax back: 219.57 is ~93–95 MHz at the estimated 4.24–4.32M cycles, and at most ~99.4 MHz even with no cycle saving, against r7s2's 105.18 and the champion's 108.66; r8s2's separate rebuild, which kept the combinational compare -> PC redirect, landed at the same 94.83 MHz with the unrelated DSP path alu_result -> xres as its worst path, so the BTB's Fmax cost is most likely not in the compare -> redirect -> PC cone that r7s2's log pointed to, but in how the ~300+ extra LUT4s (r7s2 2520, r8s2 2547, against 2205) and the LUT-RAM on the PC/io_imemAddr nets change placement across the whole design, which makes r7s2's 105.18 MHz look like a lucky placement rather than a level a re-land can get back to; this diff also did not isolate the compare as intended, because `br_tgt_q <= br_taken_ok ? pc_imm : pc_plus4` and the counter-training flops still put ~35 D-pins on branch_cond, so a registered redirect should choose its target from ID-registered bits; three BTB builds on the 108.66 MHz base have landed at 94–105 MHz, so stop spending predictor iterations on it, and try a predictor again only on the r9s1 fetch-store champion (3.88M cycles), where redirect bubbles are a larger share of cycles, with `make timing` across the scored seeds.

title: Stall-free fetch-store read address: 4 banks by pc[3:2] read pc..pc+12 every cycle, stall_if only as the last pick select
motivation:
The r9s1 champion (260.40, 3,877,238 cycles) lost ~7% Fmax against the
108.66 MHz pre-fetch-store base: placement seeds 98.22 / 100.962 /
100.962 MHz. Its logged worst path (slack -5.181 ns, arrival 15.476 ns,
13 cells, 11 logic levels) is
  u_if/u_fs/fword_q -> u_hazard (fs rs == id_ex_rd, load_use_hazard)
  -> stall_if -> u_fs ev_a/od_a index mux -> mem_e BSRAM read-address pins.
In fetch_store.sv the read candidates are A = stall ? pc : pc+4 and A+4,
so stall_if (the load-use compare, dmem stall, fetch_ok, div_busy) goes
through a 5-input index mux and then routes to BSRAM address pins, which
have a large setup time and sit away from the hazard logic. stall_if
depends on stall only because PC(t+1) = stall(t) ? pc : pc+4 is chosen
before the read. If the read covers both outcomes, stall_if does not
need to reach any BSRAM pin, and this path is gone.
